strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies concrete, practical limitations of F3Loc (lack of uncertainty modeling, dataset-specific depth training) and addresses both directly.

Sound and simple technical approach: modeling floorplan depth as heteroscedastic Laplace distributions and integrating this into the observation model of a histogram filter is clean, principled, and easy to follow; the training loss is the corresponding NLL.

Leveraging off-the-shelf pretrained depth encoders (Depth Anything V2) meaningfully improves generalization, as convincingly demonstrated by the cross-building (HGE -> CAB) experiment where F3Loc fails completely (0% SR) while UnLoc reaches 50-100% SR.

Comprehensive evaluation on three datasets (synthetic Gibson, synthetic Structured3D, real-world LaMAR HGE), with GT-depth upper bounds, multiple sequence lengths, single-frame ablations, encoder ablations (DINOv2, DepthPro, DA V2 S/B/L), runtime analysis, and grid-resolution/frequency ablations in the supplement.

Substantial and consistent empirical gains, particularly on the challenging real-world LaMAR dataset (e.g., 36.4% -> 100% SR for T=100, 1.2% -> 20% for T=15 vs. F3Loc mono), with uncertainty estimation providing a clear additional benefit beyond the stronger depth encoder.
Good qualitative analyses (depth predictions with uncertainty bands, observation likelihoods, posterior evolution) that help build intuition for why the method works.
The method retains practical properties (out-of-the-box occupancy-grid floorplans, real-time-ish runtime, graceful degradation with coarser grids) relevant to deployment.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the contribution is largely a combination of standard components — heteroscedastic Laplace NLL for uncertainty, an existing pretrained depth encoder, a masked attention head inspired by F3Loc, and the histogram filter from F3Loc. The delta over F3Loc, while effective, is incremental.

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparisons are essentially limited to F3Loc (mono/fusion) and copied results for LASER/PF-Net. Given the framing, comparisons to other floorplan methods (e.g., LaLaLoc++ under comparable settings) or to lightweight SLAM/odometry-plus-matching pipelines would strengthen claims.

Small evaluation sets on the key real-world benchmark: LaMAR HGE results are based on as few as 11 sequences at T=100 (and N=2-24 on CAB), so some reported gains (e.g., '2.7x improvement') rest on very few trajectories; variance/significance is not discussed.

The paper assumes access to relative poses between frames, gravity direction, and intrinsics; while these are typically available on AR devices, the impact of noise in ego-motion/gravity on the results is not analyzed.

Some experimental inconsistencies are not fully explained, e.g., on Gibson(t) the method with uncertainty has higher RMSE (0.16 vs 0.11 w/o uncertainty) at T=100, and on Gibson/Structured3D single-frame results uncertainty sometimes slightly hurts; the framing of uncertainty as an unqualified win is slightly stronger than the evidence.

Fairness question: F3Loc mono* on LaMAR is trained by the authors with limited data, and F3Loc's struggles may partly stem from depth-data scarcity rather than architecture; a hybrid (F3Loc + pretrained depth encoder without uncertainty) is only partially covered by 'Ours w/o Uncertainties', which conflates the encoder change and the pipeline.
Uncertainty calibration is not evaluated (e.g., do predicted b correspond to actual depth errors?), despite uncertainty being the headline contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated identification of two concrete limitations of prior art (F3Loc): lack of depth uncertainty modeling and dependence on per-environment depth networks.
Sound probabilistic formulation: depth predictions as Laplace distributions with a learned scale parameter, naturally integrated into the observation model and trained via a principled NLL loss.

Strong empirical results across synthetic and real-world benchmarks (Gibson, Structured3D, LaMAR HGE/CAB), including very large gains on the realistic LaMAR dataset (e.g., 2.7x and 16.7x on long/short sequences), with GT-depth upper bounds reported for context.

Useful ablations: encoder choice (DINOv2, DepthPro, Depth Anything V2 S/B/L), uncertainty on/off, runtime and grid-resolution analysis, observation-frequency ablation, and cross-building generalization with and without fine-tuning in the supplementary.
Comprehensive supplementary material with additional quantitative and qualitative analyses that support the main claims.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contributions are (1) adding an uncertainty output with a standard Laplace NLL loss and (2) swapping in an off-the-shelf pretrained encoder, on top of the existing F3Loc framework (masked attention, ray matching, histogram filter). Each component is well-executed but individually close to known techniques.

The method still requires per-environment training of the depth/attention head; the 'elimination of per-dataset training' claim applies mainly to the depth encoder, and the CAB experiments show fine-tuning is still needed for best results.

Uncertainty quality is never directly evaluated (e.g., calibration, whether predicted b relates to actual depth error); conclusions about uncertainty are drawn only indirectly through localization metrics, and on Gibson/Structured3D single-frame results uncertainty even slightly hurts.
Main comparisons are limited to F3Loc; other recent floorplan/localization baselines (e.g., PF-Net, LaLaLoc++) are largely cited from prior papers or omitted from sequential experiments.
Runtime increases substantially on large floorplans (~1s/frame matching cost); the mitigations (coarser grid, less frequent updates) trade off accuracy and are deferred to the supplement.
Dataset customization of LaMAR (manual floorplan modifications, filtering) complicates direct comparability with prior reported numbers, although the authors are transparent about this.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and motivates two concrete limitations of the prior state of the art (F3Loc): lack of uncertainty modeling in depth predictions and the need for per-environment depth networks, and addresses both directly.

The method is technically sound and well presented: modeling floorplan depth as Laplace distributions with learned per-ray uncertainty and integrating this into the histogram filter's observation model is a clean, principled extension.

Comprehensive evaluation on three datasets (Gibson, Structured3D, LaMAR), including synthetic and real-world data, with appropriate baselines (F3Loc mono, F3Loc fusion, LASER, PF-Net), GT-depth upper bounds, and both sequential and single-frame settings.

Strong empirical results: 2.7x and 16.7x higher recall on the challenging real-world LaMAR HGE dataset, plus successful cross-building generalization (HGE -> CAB) where F3Loc fails completely, supporting the generalization claim.

Thorough ablation studies: encoder choice (DINOv2, DepthPro, Depth Anything V2 variants), with/without uncertainty, runtime analysis, observation update frequency, and grid resolution trade-offs in the supplementary.

The ablation disentangling the two contributions (pretrained encoder vs. uncertainty) shows each helps, and uncertainty helps most precisely in the settings where it was motivated (short sequences, complex real-world environments).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and the work is heavily built on F3Loc: the masked attention, floorplan matching, and histogram filter are all inherited from prior work. The new components (a Laplace uncertainty head trained with negative log-likelihood, and swapping in a pretrained depth encoder) are relatively standard techniques; the main contribution is a well-executed combination rather than a fundamentally new approach.

The headline 2.7x improvement on LaMAR HGE at T=100 is based on only N=11 sequences (36.4% -> 100%), and other LaMAR numbers are similarly based on small test sets; statistical significance or confidence intervals are not reported, making the largest claimed gains somewhat fragile.

The uncertainty component shows limited benefit on synthetic datasets (Gibson, Structured3D) in single-frame localization, and on Gibson it slightly degrades some depth metrics (e.g., MAE and recall at fine thresholds), suggesting the benefit is scenario-dependent.

Runtime is notably higher than F3Loc mono (0.185s vs 0.015s feature extraction; matching ~0.88s on large floorplans); the argument that fewer frames are needed offsets this is reasonable but not fully quantified in wall-clock terms.
No explicit statement of code release or full training details beyond brief supplementary notes, which limits reproducibility for a method whose appeal is practical deployability.

Comparison is essentially limited to floorplan-based methods; no discussion or empirical positioning against broader sequential localization or visual odometry alternatives that do not require relative poses between frames.

strengths: Clear identification of two concrete limitations of the state-of-the-art F3Loc (lack of uncertainty modeling, dataset-specific depth networks) and a simple, principled solution for each: Laplace-distributed depth predictions with learned uncertainty, and a plug-and-play off-the-shelf monodepth encoder (Depth Anything v2)

Comprehensive evaluation: synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and real-world (LaMAR HGE, cross-building CAB) datasets, multiple sequence lengths, single-frame and sequential settings, runtime analysis, and useful ablations (encoder choice incl. DINOv2/DepthPro/DAv2 sizes, Laplace vs. Gaussian likelihood, grid resolution, observation update frequency)
Large, convincing empirical gains over F3Loc, e.g., 42.2x improvement on 15-frame sequences on LaMAR HGE, and clear generalization advantage on the unseen CAB building where F3Loc fails completely

The 'F3Loc + Depth Anything v2' baseline is a fair and important control, and the uncertainty ablation (Table 5) shows consistent improvements across all encoders, supporting the claim that uncertainty modeling contributes beyond simply using a stronger encoder

Good reproducibility: code and trained models released, training/evaluation procedures documented, dataset preprocessing and splits described in detail; honest discussion of evaluation caveats (e.g., LaMAR ground-truth alignment by affine fitting, non-strict zero-shot setting)
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core techniques are standard — aleatoric uncertainty via Laplace NLL (Nix & Weigend; Kendall & Gal), a histogram filter inherited from F3Loc, and an off-the-shelf monodepth encoder. Much of the gain over original F3Loc comes from swapping in the stronger encoder (visible in Tables 1, 2, 6), so the paper's own contribution beyond 'better features + a likelihood head' is modest

The claim of eliminating per-environment training is somewhat overstated: only the encoder is off-the-shelf; the attention/uncertainty head (and F3Loc comparably) is still trained per dataset, and the cross-dataset experiments (Tables 7-8) show fine-tuning on the target domain still yields substantial gains, contradicting a fully 'plug-and-play' narrative

LaMAR CAB generalization results rest on very small sample sizes (N=2 at T=100, N=18 at T=15), making the 100% vs. 50% claims statistically fragile; similarly small N for several LaMAR HGE length buckets (e.g., N=11)

Post-processing contributes a large share of the reported gains (e.g., +16 points SR on 15-frame Gibson sequences, sometimes even beating the GT-depth upper bound), which raises questions about how much is attributable to the core uncertainty-aware model versus a generic trajectory refinement stage applied on top

Uncertainty calibration is not evaluated: predicted uncertainties drive weighting in the filter and post-processing, but there is no analysis of whether the predicted b values are calibrated (e.g., negative log-likelihood or coverage of depth errors), which would substantiate the central uncertainty-modeling claim

Some results are difficult to interpret (UnLoc w/o post-processing exceeding GT-depth performance; RMSE(all) < RMSE(succ.) in Table 1), and the success metric over 'last 10 frames' plus post-processing can mask per-frame trajectory quality

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem (floorplan-based indoor localization) and clearly articulates the limitations of the prior state of the art (F3Loc): missing uncertainty modeling and the need for per-environment depth network training.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: synthetic (Gibson, Structured3D) and real-world (LaMAR HGE, LaMAR CAB) datasets, multiple sequence lengths, success rates and RMSE, single-frame and sequential settings, runtime analysis, and multiple ablations (encoders, uncertainty distributions, grid resolution, observation update frequency).

The ablations are informative: comparing against F3Loc with the Depth Anything v2 encoder swapped in helps isolate the contribution of the uncertainty modeling from that of a better encoder, and Table 5 shows uncertainty estimation consistently helps across encoders.

The method is well written and easy to follow; the probabilistic formulation (Laplace likelihood, uncertainty-weighted matching and post-processing) is coherent, and a reproducibility statement with code and trained models is provided.
Real-world results on LaMAR are substantial (e.g., from 1.2% to 50.6% SR on 15-frame sequences vs. F3Loc mono), and cross-building generalization (HGE to CAB) is a useful addition.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core components are individually well-established: a Laplace NLL uncertainty head is standard practice (Kendall & Gal, 2017; Nix & Weigend, 1994), the masked attention depth predictor and histogram filter are adopted from F3Loc, and the post-processing is a simple SE(2) correction. The contribution is essentially a recombination of known techniques, which weakens the case for a top-tier venue.

The headline claims rest heavily on settings where the baseline nearly fails. The '42.2x' and '2.7x' improvements are computed against F3Loc mono on LaMAR, where the authors themselves retrained the baseline and it performs close to zero; the multiplier framing inflates modest absolute gains elsewhere. On Gibson, gains over F3Loc + Depth Anything v2 are much smaller (e.g., 94.9 vs. 89.7 at T=50), and in single-frame depth MAE UnLoc is actually slightly worse (0.25 vs. 0.23 m on Gibson).

Fairness concerns regarding post-processing: the SE(2) refinement over the last k frames is a general technique that could also be applied to F3Loc, yet it is only given to UnLoc. This makes some comparisons (and the surprising result that UnLoc with post-processing exceeds even the GT-depth upper bound on 15-frame Gibson sequences) hard to attribute specifically to the proposed uncertainty modeling; exceeding the GT-depth upper bound deserves scrutiny rather than being reported as a straightforward win.

Some experimental settings have very small sample sizes, e.g., LaMAR CAB sequential localization with N=2 sequences at T=100, making the reported SR differences statistically weak and the generalization claims fragile.

Practicality is questionable on large floorplans: roughly one second per frame on LaMAR (matching dominating runtime) undercuts the claimed real-time applicability, and the arguments for why this is acceptable are somewhat hand-wavy.

The LaMAR ground-truth 2D poses rely on a manual, self-calibrated affine alignment with no independent validation, which introduces a potential source of systematic error affecting both training supervision and evaluation.

Epistemic uncertainty is deferred entirely to future work, although out-of-distribution generalization (which is a central motivation of using off-the-shelf depth models) is precisely where epistemic uncertainty matters most; the aleatoric-only treatment leaves this motivation only partially addressed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: sequential visual floorplan localization with two concrete, well-articulated limitations of the prior SOTA (F3Loc) — lack of depth uncertainty modeling and per-environment depth training.

Strong empirical results: substantial improvements over F3Loc on both synthetic (Gibson) and real-world (LaMAR HGE) data, with dramatic gains on short sequences (e.g., 42.2x on 15-frame sequences on LaMAR), which is practically relevant for time-to-localization.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple datasets (Gibson, Structured3D, LaMAR HGE/CAB), multiple sequence lengths, GT-depth upper bounds, runtime analysis, and a cross-building generalization experiment (HGE -> CAB).

Good ablations: encoder choice (DINOv2 vs. DepthPro vs. Depth Anything v2 variants), Laplace vs. Gaussian uncertainty model, uncertainty on/off, post-processing on/off, grid resolution, and observation update frequency.
Reproducibility efforts: code, trained models, dataset preprocessing, and training details are provided; the pipeline is explicitly agnostic to the depth backbone.
Uncertainty-weighted post-processing (Eq. 8) is a sensible, lightweight refinement that demonstrably helps, especially on short sequences.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is relatively incremental: the core ingredients are a standard heteroscedastic Laplace NLL (Kendall & Gal, 2017), F3Loc's histogram filter and masked attention, and an off-the-shelf Depth Anything v2 encoder. Table 1 shows that much of the gain over F3Loc mono comes simply from swapping in the pretrained encoder (86.5 -> 94.6 SR@1m), with uncertainty and post-processing adding further but more modest improvements.

No direct evaluation of uncertainty quality: the paper claims uncertainty reflects aleatoric ambiguity (glass walls, doorways, featureless walls), but there are no calibration metrics, reliability diagrams, or correlation analyses between predicted uncertainty and depth error — only qualitative visualizations (Fig. 3, 5). The central claim that 'uncertainty-aware' weighting is the cause of the gains is therefore only indirectly supported.

Some test sets are very small, limiting statistical significance: LaMAR HGE has only N=11 sequences at T=100 and the cross-building CAB evaluation has as few as N=2 sequences at T=100 (Table 7), where 50.0 vs. 100.0 SR corresponds to a single sequence.

The baseline comparison is narrow: essentially F3Loc (in mono and fusion variants) plus stale LASER numbers copied from Chen et al. (2024a). No comparison against other recent indoor localization or probabilistic-filtering approaches.

Several dependencies are assumed (gravity direction, camera intrinsics, ego-motion between frames); the GeoCalib fallback is mentioned but not evaluated, so robustness to noisy versions of these inputs is unknown.

Reproducibility statement contains an empty/placeholder URL in the manuscript; training details (e.g., no learning-rate schedule, no validation protocol, single run without variance reporting) are thin.

The abstract's headline multipliers (2.7x / 42.2x) are driven by the weakest configurations (F3Loc mono on LaMAR), which slightly overstates the practical improvement over the best competing setup (F3Loc + Depth Anything v2).
